{{Short description|Unexpected outcome in experiments}}
In [[science]], a '''null result''' is a result without the expected content: that is, the proposed result is absent.<ref>{{cite journal |first=C. |last=Giunti |title=New ordering principle for the classical statistical analysis of Poisson processes with background |journal=[[Physical Review|Phys. Rev. D]] |volume=59 |issue=5 |article-number=053001 |year=1999 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.59.053001 |arxiv=hep-ph/9808240 |bibcode=1999PhRvD..59e3001G |s2cid=14948954 |display-authors=etal}}</ref> It is an experimental outcome which does not show an otherwise expected effect. This does not imply a result of zero or nothing, simply a result that does not support the [[hypothesis]].

In [[statistical hypothesis testing]], a null result occurs when an experimental result is not significantly different from what is to be expected under the [[null hypothesis]]; its probability (under the null hypothesis) does not exceed the [[significance level]], i.e., the threshold set prior to testing for rejection of the null hypothesis. The significance level varies, but common choices include 0.10, 0.05, and 0.01.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Casella|first1=George|title=Statistical Inference|last2=Berger|first2=Roger|publisher=Duxbury|year=2002|isbn=0-534-24312-6|edition=2nd|page=385}}</ref> However, a non-significant result does not necessarily mean that an effect is absent.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lakens |first=Daniël |date=2017 |title=Equivalence Tests: A Practical Primer for t Tests, Correlations, and Meta-Analyses |journal=Social Psychological and Personality Science |language=en |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=355–362 |doi=10.1177/1948550617697177 |issn=1948-5506 |pmc=5502906 |pmid=28736600}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gross |first=Justin H. |date=2015 |title=Testing What Matters (If You Must Test at All): A Context-Driven Approach to Substantive and Statistical Significance |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ajps.12149 |journal=American Journal of Political Science |language=en |volume=59 |issue=3 |pages=775–788 |doi=10.1111/ajps.12149 |issn=0092-5853|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hartman |first1=Erin |last2=Hidalgo |first2=F. Daniel |date=2018 |title=An Equivalence Approach to Balance and Placebo Tests |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ajps.12387 |journal=American Journal of Political Science |language=en |volume=62 |issue=4 |pages=1000–1013 |doi=10.1111/ajps.12387 |issn=0092-5853|hdl=1721.1/126115 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rainey |first=Carlisle |date=2014 |title=Arguing for a Negligible Effect |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ajps.12102 |journal=American Journal of Political Science |language=en |volume=58 |issue=4 |pages=1083–1091 |doi=10.1111/ajps.12102 |issn=0092-5853|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

As an example in [[physics]], the results of the [[Michelson–Morley experiment]] were of this type, as it did not detect the expected velocity relative to the postulated [[luminiferous aether]]. This experiment's famous failed detection, commonly referred to as the ''null result'', contributed to the development of [[special relativity]]. The experiment did appear to measure a non-zero "drift", but the value was far too small to account for the theoretically expected results; it is generally thought to be inside the [[Noise (signal processing)|noise]] level of the experiment.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://hsc.csu.edu.au/physics/core/space/9_2_4/924net.html#net4 |title=Role of the Michelson-Morley experiments in making determinations about competing theories |access-date=2003-07-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121107000031/http://hsc.csu.edu.au/physics/core/space/9_2_4/924net.html#net4 |archive-date=2012-11-07 }}</ref>

==Publishing bias==
Despite similar quality of execution and [[Design of experiments|design]],<ref name="Easterbrook">{{cite journal |last1=Easterbrook |first1=P. J. |last2=Berlin |first2=J. A. |last3=Gopalan |first3=R. |last4=Matthews |first4=D. R. |year=1991 |title=Publication bias in clinical research |journal=[[Lancet (journal)|Lancet]] |volume=337 |issue=8746 |pages=867–872 |doi=10.1016/0140-6736(91)90201-Y |pmid=1672966 |s2cid=36570135 |doi-access=free}}</ref> papers with statistically significant results are three times more likely to be published than those with null results.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dickersin |first1=K. |author-link=Kay Dickersin |last2=Chan |first2=S. |last3=Chalmers |first3=T. C. |display-authors=etal |year=1987 |title=Publication bias and clinical trials |journal=[[Controlled Clinical Trials]] |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=343–353 |doi=10.1016/0197-2456(87)90155-3 |pmid=3442991}}</ref> This unduly motivates researchers to manipulate their practices to ensure statistically significant results, such as by [[data dredging]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pearce |first1=J |last2=Derrick |first2=B |date=2019 |title=Preliminary testing: The devil of statistics? |journal=Reinvention: An International Journal of Undergraduate Research |volume=12 |issue=2 |doi=10.31273/reinvention.v12i2.339 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Many factors contribute to publication bias.<ref name="Rothstein2005">H. Rothstein, A. J. Sutton and M. Borenstein. (2005). ''Publication bias in meta-analysis: prevention, assessment and adjustments''. Wiley. Chichester, England; Hoboken, NJ.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chopra |first1=Felix |last2=Haaland |first2=Ingar |last3=Roth |first3=Christopher |last4=Stegmann |first4=Andreas |date=2023 |title=The Null Result Penalty |journal=The Economic Journal |volume=134 |issue=657 |pages=193–219 |doi=10.1093/ej/uead060 |issn=0013-0133}}</ref> For instance, once a scientific finding is well established, it may become newsworthy to publish reliable papers that fail to reject the null hypothesis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Luijendijk |first1=HJ |last2=Koolman |first2=X |date=May 2012 |title=The incentive to publish negative studies: how beta-blockers and depression got stuck in the publication cycle. |journal=J Clin Epidemiol |volume=65 |issue=5 |pages=488–92 |doi=10.1016/j.jclinepi.2011.06.022 |pmid=22342262}}</ref> Most commonly, investigators simply decline to submit results, leading to [[non-response bias]]. Investigators may also assume they made a mistake, find that the null result fails to support a known finding, lose interest in the topic, or anticipate that others will be uninterested in the null results.<ref name="Easterbrook" />

There are several scientific journals dedicated to the publication of negative or null results, including the following:
* ''[[Journal of Negative Results in Biomedicine]]'' (defunct)
* ''[[Journal of Pharmaceutical Negative Results]]''
* ''[[Journal of Unsolved Questions]]''

While it is not exclusively dedicated to publishing negative results, [[BioMed Central|BMC Research Notes]] also publishes negative results in the form of research or data notes.
